decks.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Part 1: Potential and potential energy
goals: Define electric potential and potential difference and find the potential of a point charge, a dipole and a system of charges
Relate equipotential surfaces to field lines and use E = −dV/dr
Calculate the potential energy of a system of charges and of a dipole in a uniform field

slides.heading: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
slides.body_md: Part 1 — describing the electric field with a single number at each point, the **potential**, and the energy stored in arrangements of charges.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: work against the field, potential, equipotential surfaces, potential energy

slides.narration: A field is a vector at every point, which makes calculations heavy. In this part we replace it with a single number at each point, the electric potential, found from the work needed to bring a charge there. Potential makes energy problems easy. We will meet equipotential surfaces, link potential to field, and find the energy stored in a group of charges and in a dipole placed in a field.

slides.heading: Electric potential and potential difference
slides.body_md:
The electrostatic force is **conservative**: the work done in moving a charge between two points does not depend on the path. So we can define
$$V_B - V_A = \dfrac{W_{A \to B}}{q},$$
the work done **by an external agent** per unit positive charge in moving it slowly from A to B. The **potential** at a point is the work per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity ($V_\infty = 0$). Unit: **volt**, $1\ \text{V} = 1\ \text{J C}^{-1}$.
bullets: Potential is a scalar: potentials of several charges simply add.
A positive charge moves on its own from high to low potential; a negative charge from low to high.

slides.narration: Because the electrostatic force is conservative, the work done in carrying a charge from one point to another depends only on the end points. The work done per unit positive charge by an outside agent is the potential difference between those points. Taking infinity as zero, the potential at a point is the work per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity. One volt is one joule per coulomb. In the figure, potential falls along the field.

slides.heading: Potential of a point charge
slides.body_md:
Bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to distance $r$ from $q$:
$$V(r) = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{q}{r} = \dfrac{kq}{r}$$
Positive near a positive charge, negative near a negative one; it falls as $1/r$, more slowly than the field ($1/r^2$).
bullets: $V$ has a sign; $E$ is a magnitude with a direction.
For a system of charges: $V = k\sum_i \dfrac{q_i}{r_i}$ (algebraic sum).

visual.alt: Graph comparing the potential of a point charge, falling as one over r, with its field, falling faster as one over r squared
visual.caption: Point charge: both are 1 at r = 1; the field falls off faster.

slides.narration: For a point charge, the potential at distance r is k q over r. It keeps the sign of the charge, so it is positive near a positive charge and negative near a negative one. Notice the graph: the potential falls as one over r, while the field falls faster, as one over r squared. For several charges, just add the potentials with their signs. No vector addition is needed.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: potential of two charges
slides.body_md: Charges $+4$ nC and $-2$ nC are $20$ cm apart. Find (a) the potential at the midpoint, (b) the points on the line joining them where $V = 0$.
bullets: (b) Between them, $x$ from $+4$ nC: $\dfrac{4}{x} = \dfrac{2}{0.20 - x}$, so $x = 0.13$ m (13.3 cm).
Outside, beyond $-2$ nC: $\dfrac{4}{x} = \dfrac{2}{x - 0.20}$, so $x = 0.40$ m from $+4$ nC (20 cm beyond $-2$ nC).
Check — potentials add as numbers, so there can be two zero points; the **field** is not zero at either.

visual.alt: Worked table: 180 volts at the midpoint and zero potential at 13.3 centimetres and at 40 centimetres from the positive charge

slides.narration: Potentials are scalars, so at the midpoint just add k q over r for each charge with its sign: one hundred and eighty volts. To find where the potential is zero, set the two contributions equal in size. Between the charges this happens nearer the smaller charge, at thirteen point three centimetres from the larger one. There is a second zero point outside, beyond the negative charge. The field is not zero at these points.

slides.heading: Potential of an electric dipole
slides.body_md: At distance $r$ from the centre, at angle $\theta$ to the dipole axis ($r \gg a$):
columns:
$$V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$$
- On the axis ($\theta = 0^\circ$): $V = \dfrac{kp}{r^2}$.
- On the equatorial line ($\theta = 90^\circ$): $V = 0$.

**Compared with a point charge**
- Depends on direction ($\cos\theta$), not just on $r$.
- Falls as $1/r^2$, faster than $1/r$.
- On the equatorial plane $V = 0$ although $E \neq 0$.

visual.alt: Closed equipotential curves around each charge of a dipole and a straight zero-potential line midway
visual.caption: Traced numerically: the potential stays constant along each dashed curve.

slides.narration: For a dipole the potential far away is k p cos theta over r squared. On the axis it is k p over r squared. On the equatorial line it is zero, because every point there is the same distance from the two equal and opposite charges. That is a classic trap: zero potential does not mean zero field. The equatorial line has a field pointing opposite to the dipole moment.

slides.heading: Quick check: zero potential, zero field?
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason.
slides.narration: Think of the equatorial line of a dipole. Work out the potential there and recall the direction of the field.

slides.heading: Equipotential surfaces
slides.body_md: An **equipotential surface** has the same potential at every point.
bullets: No work is done in moving a charge along it ($W = q\Delta V = 0$).
The field is **perpendicular** to it at every point; otherwise a component along the surface would do work.
Field lines point from higher to lower equipotentials.
Two equipotentials never intersect.

slides.narration: Join all points that have the same potential and you get an equipotential surface. Moving a charge along such a surface takes no work, because the potential difference is zero. That forces the field to be at right angles to the surface everywhere. For a point charge the surfaces are spheres. Equal potential steps are further apart far away, because the field is weaker there.

slides.heading: Equipotentials of a dipole and of a uniform field
slides.body_md: For a uniform field the equipotentials are **parallel planes** perpendicular to $\vec E$. For a dipole they are closed curves around each charge, with the $V = 0$ plane midway.

visual.alt: Closed equipotential curves around each charge of a dipole and a straight zero-potential line midway
visual.caption: Traced numerically: the potential stays constant along each dashed curve.

slides.narration: In a uniform field, such as between two large plates, the equipotentials are flat planes at right angles to the field, equally spaced for equal steps of potential. Around a dipole they form closed loops round each charge, positive round the positive charge and negative round the negative one. The plane midway between the charges is at zero potential. Field lines would cross every one of these curves at right angles.

slides.heading: Field from potential
slides.body_md:
Moving a small distance $dl$ along $\vec E$, the potential drops by $dV = -E\,dl$. So
$$E = -\dfrac{dV}{dl}\quad \text{(along the direction of steepest fall)},\qquad E = \dfrac{\Delta V}{d}\ \text{in a uniform field.}$$
bullets: $\vec E$ points in the direction in which $V$ **decreases** fastest.
Closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field.
Unit check: V m$^{-1}$ = N C$^{-1}$.

slides.narration: The field and the potential are linked by a slope. The field equals minus the rate at which potential changes with distance, taken along the direction where it falls fastest. In a uniform field this becomes the potential difference divided by the distance between the planes. So crowded equipotentials mean a strong field, and volts per metre is the same unit as newtons per coulomb.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: work and potential difference
slides.body_md: (a) A charge of $+2.0\,\mu\text{C}$ is moved from A ($V_A = 50$ V) to B ($V_B = -30$ V). Find the work done by an external agent and by the field. (b) In a uniform field of 500 V m$^{-1}$, find the potential difference between planes 4.0 cm apart.
bullets: The field does $W_\text{field} = -W_\text{ext} = 1.6 \times 10^{-4}$ J: a positive charge moves "downhill" in potential by itself.
(b) $\Delta V = Ed = 500 \times 0.040 = 20$ V, the higher plane being further **up-field**.

slides.narration: Work by an external agent is the charge times the change in potential, final minus initial. Here the potential falls by eighty volts, so the agent does negative work, minus one point six times ten to the minus four joule, and the field does the same amount of positive work. In a uniform field, the potential difference is simply field times distance, so five hundred volts per metre over four centimetres gives twenty volts.

slides.heading: Potential energy of a system of charges
slides.body_md:
The potential energy of a system is the work done to assemble it from charges at infinity. For two charges:
$$U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\,\dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r_{12}}$$
For three charges, add over the **pairs**: $U = k\left(\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}} + \dfrac{q_1q_3}{r_{13}} + \dfrac{q_2q_3}{r_{23}}\right)$.
bullets: $U > 0$ for like charges (work needed to push them together).
$U < 0$ for unlike charges (the system is bound; work is needed to separate them).
A charge $q$ in an external potential $V$ has $U = qV$.

A charge in an outside potential V has energy q V.

bullets: Step 2 — sum of products $= (1 - 2 - 2) \times 10^{-12} = -3.0 \times 10^{-12}$ C².

slides.narration: Count the pairs: there are three. One pair has two positive charges and two pairs are positive with negative. Because all distances are equal, add the products of the charges first, getting minus three times ten to the minus twelve. Multiply by nine times ten to the nine and divide by the side. The energy is minus zero point two seven joule, so the system is bound.

slides.heading: A dipole in a uniform field: potential energy
slides.body_md: Taking $U = 0$ when the dipole is perpendicular to the field:
columns:
**Work to rotate**
$$W = U(\theta_2) - U(\theta_1) = pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$$
Turning a dipole from $0^\circ$ to $180^\circ$ needs $W = 2pE$.

visual.alt: Table of dipole potential energy at 0, 90 and 180 degrees: minus p E stable, zero, plus p E unstable

slides.narration: A dipole in a uniform field has potential energy minus p E cos theta. It is lowest, minus p E, when the dipole points along the field, which is the stable position. It is highest, plus p E, when it points against the field, which is unstable. The work needed to turn the dipole is the change in this energy, so turning it all the way round from aligned to reversed takes two p E.

slides.heading: Quick check: rotating a dipole
slides.body_md: Find the work needed to rotate a dipole from the stable position by 180°.
slides.narration: Use the energy at the start and at the end of the rotation, with U equals minus p E cos theta.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

visual.alt: Summary table of potential difference, potential of a point charge and a dipole, field from potential, energy of two charges and of a dipole in a field

slides.narration: To sum up: potential is work per unit charge, measured in volts, and it adds as a plain number. A point charge gives k q over r; a dipole gives k p cos theta over r squared, zero on its equatorial plane. The field is at right angles to equipotentials and equals the rate at which potential falls. Systems of charges store energy k q one q two over r per pair, and a dipole in a field has energy minus p E cos theta.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Keep the **signs** of charges in $V$ and $U$; leave them out only in Coulomb-force magnitudes.
Work by the agent $= q(V_\text{final} - V_\text{initial})$; work by the field is the negative of that.
$V = 0$ does not imply $E = 0$, and $E = 0$ does not imply $V = 0$.
For energy of a system, count each **pair once**.

visual.alt: Table of traps and fixes: add potentials as signed numbers, count pairs once, sign of work

slides.narration: Signs carry the physics in this chapter, so keep them in every potential and energy calculation. Work by an outside agent is the charge times final minus initial potential. Do not assume that zero potential means zero field or the other way round. When finding the energy of a group of charges, count each pair once: three charges have three pairs, four charges have six.

slides.heading: Conductors, dielectrics and capacitors
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how charge behaves on conductors and inside insulators, and how a capacitor stores charge and energy.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: conductors, dielectrics, capacitance, parallel plates, combinations and stored energy

slides.narration: Every phone charger, camera flash and ceiling-fan regulator contains capacitors. To understand them we first see how charge settles on conductors and how insulating materials respond to a field. Then we define capacitance, derive it for parallel plates with and without a dielectric, combine capacitors in series and in parallel, and find the energy a charged capacitor stores.

slides.heading: Electrostatics of conductors
slides.body_md: In a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium:
bullets: The field **inside** the material is zero.
Any excess charge resides on the **outer surface**.
Just outside, the field is **normal** to the surface, with $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$.
The whole conductor (surface and inside) is at **one potential**.
A charge-free **cavity** inside a conductor has zero field: **electrostatic shielding**.

slides.narration: A conductor has free electrons. If there were any field inside, they would move until the field vanished, so in equilibrium the field inside is zero. Excess charge pushes itself out to the surface. The field just outside must be at right angles to the surface, otherwise charges would slide along it, and its value is sigma over epsilon nought. The whole body is one equipotential, and an empty cavity inside is shielded from outside fields.

slides.heading: Potential of a charged conducting sphere
slides.body_md: For a sphere (or thin shell) of radius $R$ with charge $q$: outside $V = kq/r$; on and inside the surface $V = kq/R$, constant, because $E = 0$ inside.

visual.alt: Graph of potential against distance for a charged thin shell or conducting sphere: constant inside and equal to its surface value, then falling as one over r outside
visual.caption: Inside, E = 0, so V does not change.

slides.narration: Here is the potential of a charged conducting sphere. Outside, it behaves like a point charge at the centre, so the potential falls as one over r. At the surface it is k q over R. Inside, the field is zero, so no work is needed to move a charge around, and the potential stays at its surface value everywhere inside. Compare this flat graph with the field graph from Chapter one, which drops to zero inside.

slides.heading: Dielectrics and polarisation
slides.body_md: A **dielectric** is an insulator. In a field its molecules become (or line up as) dipoles: the material is **polarised**. The dipole moment per unit volume is the **polarisation** $\vec P$; for most materials it is proportional to the field.
bullets: **Non-polar** molecules (no permanent dipole): the field induces dipoles by shifting charges.
**Polar** molecules (water): permanent dipoles, partly lined up by the field.
Net effect: bound surface charges that **oppose** the applied field, so the field inside is reduced to $E_0/K$.

In non-polar materials the field pulls the electron clouds slightly away from the nuclei, creating tiny induced dipoles. In polar materials the permanent dipoles turn partly into line. Either way, a layer of bound negative charge appears on the face near the positive plate and positive charge on the other face, reducing the field inside by the dielectric constant K.

slides.heading: Capacitors and capacitance
slides.body_md:
A **capacitor** is two conductors separated by an insulator, carrying $+Q$ and $-Q$. The potential difference $V$ between them is proportional to $Q$:
$$C = \dfrac{Q}{V},\qquad \text{unit farad (F)} = \text{C V}^{-1}$$
$C$ depends only on the size, shape and separation of the conductors and the medium between them.
bullets: 1 F is huge; practical values are μF ($10^{-6}$ F), nF and pF ($10^{-12}$ F).
A large $C$ stores a large charge at a small voltage.

slides.narration: A capacitor is any pair of conductors separated by an insulator. Charge one with plus Q and the other with minus Q, and a potential difference V appears between them, proportional to Q. The ratio Q over V is the capacitance, measured in farads. It depends on geometry and the material between the conductors, not on the charge. A farad is enormous; real capacitors are microfarads or picofarads.

slides.heading: Parallel-plate capacitor
slides.body_md: Plates of area $A$, separation $d$ (small compared with the plate size), charge $\pm Q$, $\sigma = Q/A$. Between the plates the two sheet fields add:
bullets: Outside the plates the sheet fields cancel, so $E \approx 0$.
Bigger plates or a smaller gap give a larger capacitance.

slides.narration: For two large parallel plates, each plate acts like a charged sheet. Between them the two sheet fields add to sigma over epsilon nought, and outside they cancel. The field is uniform, so the potential difference is field times separation. Divide the charge by this voltage and you get epsilon nought A over d. Larger plates or a narrower gap mean more capacitance.

slides.heading: Effect of a dielectric
slides.body_md:
Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant $K$ reduces the field (for the same $Q$) from $E_0$ to $E_0/K$, so $V$ falls by $K$ and
$$C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = K C_0$$
A slab of thickness $t < d$ gives $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d - t + t/K}$.
bullets: With the battery **disconnected**: $Q$ fixed, $V$ and $E$ fall by $K$.
With the battery **connected**: $V$ fixed, $Q$ rises by $K$.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a parallel-plate capacitor
slides.body_md: Plates of area $0.020$ m² are $1.0$ mm apart in air. Find $C$, the charge at 100 V, and $C$ when the gap is filled with a dielectric of $K = 5$.
bullets: Step 1 — $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d} = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.020}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.77 \times 10^{-10}$ F $= 177$ pF.
Step 3 — with the dielectric: $C = 5 \times 177 = 885$ pF.

visual.alt: Worked table: 177 picofarads in air, 17.7 nanocoulombs at 100 volts, 885 picofarads with the dielectric

slides.narration: Convert the gap to metres, one times ten to the minus three. Then epsilon nought A over d gives one hundred and seventy seven picofarads, a typical small capacitor even with a large plate area. At one hundred volts the charge is seventeen point seven nanocoulombs. Filling the gap with a dielectric of constant five multiplies the capacitance by five, to eight hundred and eighty five picofarads.

slides.heading: Combining capacitors
slides.body_md: Series and parallel rules:
bullets: **Series:** same charge $Q$ on each; voltages add: $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dots$ (smaller than the smallest).
**Parallel:** same voltage $V$ across each; charges add: $C = C_1 + C_2 + \dots$

slides.heading: Worked example 5: a mixed network
slides.body_md: $C_1 = 3\,\mu\text{F}$ and $C_2 = 6\,\mu\text{F}$ are in series; this pair is in parallel with $C_3 = 4\,\mu\text{F}$; the network is across a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance and the charge and voltage on each.
bullets: Step 1 — series pair: $C_s = \dfrac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = 2\,\mu\text{F}$; total $C = 2 + 4 = 6\,\mu\text{F}$; $Q_\text{total} = 72\,\mu\text{C}$.
Step 2 — series branch: $Q = 2 \times 12 = 24\,\mu\text{C}$ on both $C_1$ and $C_2$; $V_1 = 24/3 = 8$ V, $V_2 = 24/6 = 4$ V.

visual.alt: Worked table: the 3 and 6 microfarad capacitors each carry 24 microcoulombs at 8 and 4 volts; the 4 microfarad carries 48 microcoulombs at 12 volts

slides.narration: Reduce the network step by step. Three and six microfarads in series give two. Adding the four microfarads in parallel gives six, so the battery supplies seventy two microcoulombs. The series branch carries twenty four microcoulombs on each capacitor, splitting the twelve volts as eight and four: the smaller capacitor takes the bigger voltage. The four microfarad capacitor has the full twelve volts and forty eight microcoulombs.

slides.heading: Energy stored in a capacitor
slides.body_md:
Charging a capacitor means moving charge against the growing voltage. The stored energy (formula only; no derivation required):
$$U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}QV$$
The energy is stored in the **electric field** between the plates.
bullets: Use $\tfrac{1}{2}CV^2$ when $V$ is fixed (battery connected), $Q^2/2C$ when $Q$ is fixed (isolated).
A camera flash stores energy slowly in a capacitor and releases it in a fraction of a millisecond.

visual.alt: Straight-line graph of voltage against charge for a 2 microfarad capacitor; the area under the line up to Q equals the stored energy one half Q V
visual.caption: Area under the V–Q line = stored energy.

slides.narration: As charge builds up, the voltage rises in proportion, so each extra bit of charge needs a little more work. The total work, the area under the voltage against charge line, is one half Q V. Using Q equals C V this can be written one half C V squared or Q squared over two C. Choose the form that matches what is held fixed. The energy is stored in the field between the plates.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: energy stored and shared
slides.body_md: A $6.0\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor is charged to 12 V. (a) Find the energy stored. (b) It is disconnected and joined to an identical uncharged capacitor. Find the total energy afterwards.
bullets: (b) Charge $Q = 72\,\mu\text{C}$ is shared: 36 μC each, $V = 6$ V. Total $U = 2 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 6^2 = 2.16 \times 10^{-4}$ J.
Half the energy is lost — as heat in the connecting wires and as radiation — even though charge is conserved.

visual.alt: Worked table: before sharing 72 microcoulombs at 12 volts, 432 microjoules; after sharing the same charge at 6 volts, 216 microjoules

slides.narration: One half C V squared gives four hundred and thirty two microjoules. When the charged capacitor is joined to an identical empty one, the seventy two microcoulombs spread equally, so each has thirty six at six volts. Add the two energies and you get only two hundred and sixteen microjoules. Charge is conserved but energy is not: half is lost as heat and radiation while the charge flows.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Always ask: is the battery **connected** (V fixed) or **disconnected** (Q fixed)? Then track C, Q, V, E and U.
Series: same Q, smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage. Parallel: same V.
Convert μF, pF, mm and cm² to SI before substituting.
The derivation asked is $C = \varepsilon_0 A/d$ (and $K\varepsilon_0 A/d$); the energy formula is used without derivation.

notes.title: Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Potential and potential difference
sections.body_md:
The electrostatic force is **conservative**, so the work done in moving a charge between two points is independent of the path.

- **Potential difference:** $V_B - V_A = W_{A\to B}/q$, the work done by an external agent per unit positive charge (moved slowly, without acceleration).
- **Potential at a point:** work per unit charge to bring a test charge from infinity ($V_\infty = 0$). Unit **volt** ($1\ \text{V} = 1\ \text{J C}^{-1}$). A scalar.
- **Point charge:** $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q}{r}$.
- **System of charges:** $V = k\sum q_i/r_i$, an algebraic (signed) sum.
- **Dipole** ($r \gg a$): $V = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$; on the axis $kp/r^2$, on the equatorial plane **0**.
- **Charged shell or conducting sphere** (radius $R$): $V = kq/r$ outside; $V = kq/R$ everywhere on and inside.

key_terms.definition_md: Work done per unit positive test charge in bringing it from infinity to the point.
One joule of work per coulomb of charge.

visual.alt: Graph comparing the potential of a point charge, falling as one over r, with its field, falling faster as one over r squared
visual.caption: Point charge: both are 1 at r = 1; the field falls off faster.

visuals.alt: Graph of potential against distance for a charged thin shell or conducting sphere: constant inside and equal to its surface value, then falling as one over r outside
visuals.caption: Inside, E = 0, so V does not change.

sections.heading: 2. Equipotential surfaces and the field
sections.body_md:
An **equipotential surface** has the same potential everywhere on it.

- No work is done in moving a charge along it.
- $\vec E$ is **perpendicular** to it at every point and points towards **lower** potential.
- Equipotentials never intersect.
- Shapes: point charge → concentric spheres; uniform field → parallel planes perpendicular to $\vec E$; dipole → closed surfaces round each charge with the $V = 0$ plane midway.

**Field from potential:** $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dl}$ along the direction of greatest decrease. In a uniform field $E = \Delta V/d$. Closely spaced equipotentials mean a strong field. V m$^{-1}$ = N C$^{-1}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A surface on which the potential has the same value at every point.
Rate of change of potential with distance; the field is its negative.

sections.heading: 3. Potential energy
sections.body_md:
**Two charges:** $U = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}}$ (work to bring them from infinity to separation $r_{12}$). Positive for like charges, negative for unlike (bound).

**Three or more charges:** sum over every **pair** once, e.g. $U = k\left(\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}} + \dfrac{q_1q_3}{r_{13}} + \dfrac{q_2q_3}{r_{23}}\right)$.

**Charge in an external potential:** $U = qV(\vec r)$. Two charges in an external field: $U = q_1V(\vec r_1) + q_2V(\vec r_2) + \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r_{12}}$.

**Dipole in a uniform field:** $U(\theta) = -pE\cos\theta = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$. Minimum $-pE$ at $\theta = 0$ (stable); maximum $+pE$ at $180^\circ$ (unstable). Work to rotate from $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$: $pE(\cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2)$.

*Electron volt:* $1\ \text{eV} = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J, the energy gained by an electron through 1 V.

key_terms.definition_md: Work done in assembling the charges from infinite separation.
Energy gained by a charge $e$ moving through a potential difference of 1 V; $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ J.

sections.heading: 5. Dielectrics and polarisation
sections.body_md:
A **dielectric** is an insulator. In an external field:

- **non-polar** molecules (O₂, H₂) acquire **induced** dipoles;
- **polar** molecules (H₂O, HCl) have permanent dipoles that partly **align** with the field (opposed by thermal motion).

The material becomes **polarised**: dipole moment per unit volume $\vec P$, proportional to $\vec E$ for most materials. Bound charges appear on the surfaces facing the plates and produce a field opposite to the applied one, so the field inside is reduced: $E = E_0/K$, where $K$ (or $\varepsilon_r$) is the **dielectric constant**. $\varepsilon = K\varepsilon_0$.

key_terms.definition_md: Dipole moment per unit volume of a dielectric in a field.
The factor $K$ by which a dielectric reduces the field (and increases the capacitance).

sections.heading: 6. Capacitors and capacitance
sections.body_md:
A capacitor: two conductors with charges $+Q$ and $-Q$ separated by an insulator. $C = Q/V$, unit **farad** (μF, nF, pF in practice).

**Parallel plates** (area $A$, gap $d$): field between plates $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ (sheet fields add; outside they cancel), $V = Qd/\varepsilon_0A$, so $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. With a dielectric filling the gap: $C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. Slab of thickness $t$: $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d - t + t/K}$.

**Combinations:**

| | Series | Parallel |
|---|---|---|
| Same on each | charge $Q$ | voltage $V$ |
| Adds | voltages | charges |
| Equivalent | $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dots$ | $C = C_1 + C_2 + \dots$ |

Two in series: $C = \dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}$; the smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage.

key_terms.definition_md: Charge stored per unit potential difference, $C = Q/V$.
Capacitance that stores 1 C at 1 V.

sections.heading: 7. Energy stored in a capacitor
sections.body_md:
$$U = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C} = \dfrac{1}{2}CV^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}QV$$
(formula used without derivation; it is the area under the V–Q line). The energy resides in the field between the plates.

**Inserting a dielectric (constant K):**

| | Battery connected (V fixed) | Battery disconnected (Q fixed) |
|---|---|---|
| C | × K | × K |
| Q | × K | unchanged |
| V | unchanged | ÷ K |
| U | × K | ÷ K |

**Sharing charge** between two capacitors conserves charge but always loses energy (heat and radiation in the wires). Two identical capacitors, one charged: half the energy is lost.

key_terms.definition_md: The final voltage when charged capacitors are joined: total charge divided by total capacitance.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Keep signs in potentials and energies; add potentials as numbers, not vectors.
- Work by an agent $= q(V_f - V_i)$; along an equipotential it is zero.
- **Connected or disconnected?** Decide first in every dielectric or plate-separation question.
- Series: same Q; parallel: same V. Check that the series result is smaller than the smallest capacitor.
- Convert pF ($10^{-12}$), nF ($10^{-9}$), μF ($10^{-6}$), mm and cm² before substituting.

cards.back_md: Work done by an external agent per unit positive charge in moving it from one point to the other: $V_B - V_A = W/q$.

cards.front_md: Potential on the equatorial plane of a dipole?
cards.back_md: Zero (but the field is not zero).

cards.front_md: Potential inside a charged conducting sphere?
cards.back_md: Constant, equal to the surface value $kq/R$.

cards.front_md: Why is no work done along an equipotential?
Angle between field lines and equipotentials?

cards.back_md: Parallel planes perpendicular to the field.

cards.front_md: Why can two equipotentials never cross?
cards.back_md: The crossing point would have two different potentials.

cards.back_md: Unlike charges: the system is bound; work must be done to separate them.

cards.front_md: Number of pair terms for four charges?
Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field?
Work to turn a dipole from 0° to 180°?
Field inside a conductor in equilibrium?

Polar: permanent molecular dipoles (water). Non-polar: dipoles only induced by the field (oxygen).

cards.front_md: Effect of a dielectric on the field between plates (same Q)?

cards.back_md: $C = C_1 + C_2 + \dots$; same voltage across each.

questions.stem_md: Find the electric potential 30 cm from a point charge of +2.0 nC in air, in volts.
questions.solution_md: $V = \dfrac{kq}{r} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-9}}{0.30} = 60$ V.

questions.stem_md: Charges $+q$, $+q$, $-q$ and $-q$ are placed at the corners of a square (the two positive charges at adjacent corners). At the centre of the square
questions.solution_md: All four charges are equally far from the centre, so the potentials cancel: $V = 0$. The fields of the two positive charges point away from them and those of the negative charges towards them; they add to a field pointing from the positive side to the negative side — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At a point on the equatorial line of an electric dipole the potential is zero, but the electric field is not zero.

**Reason (R):** Potential is a scalar, so the equal and opposite contributions cancel, whereas the fields are vectors whose components along the dipole axis add.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: the two potentials $\pm kq/\sqrt{r^2+a^2}$ cancel, while the axial components of the two fields add to $kp/(r^2+a^2)^{3/2}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Find the work done by an external agent in slowly moving a charge of +3.0 μC from a point at 20 V to a point at 80 V. Give your answer in millijoules (mJ).
At a certain point near an isolated point charge, the potential is 500 V and the field is 250 N C$^{-1}$. The distance of the point from the charge is
questions.solution_md: $V = kq/r$ and $E = kq/r^2$, so $r = V/E = 500/250 = 2$ m — option (c). (Then $q = Vr/k \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-7}$ C.)

questions.stem_md: The potential at a point on the axis of a short dipole, a distance $r$ from its centre, is $V$. At the same distance, on a line making $60^\circ$ with the axis, the potential is
questions.solution_md: $V(\theta) = kp\cos\theta/r^2$ and $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A hollow metal sphere of radius 10 cm is charged so that the potential at its surface is 450 V. The potential at a point 5 cm from its centre is
questions.solution_md: Inside a conductor $E = 0$, so the potential is the same as at the surface — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A positive charge released from rest in an electric field moves from a region of lower potential to a region of higher potential.
questions.solution_md: False. The field points towards lower potential, so a free positive charge moves from higher to lower potential (a negative charge does the opposite).

questions.stem_md: One volt is equal to one ___ per coulomb.
questions.solution_md: One **joule** per coulomb: 1 V is the potential difference across which 1 C gains or loses 1 J.

questions.stem_md: Charges of +1, +2, −3 and +4 nC are placed at the corners of a square of side 20 cm. Find the potential at the centre of the square, in volts (to 3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: Each corner is $0.10\sqrt{2} = 0.141$ m from the centre. $V = \dfrac{k(q_1 + q_2 + q_3 + q_4)}{r} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 4 \times 10^{-9}}{0.1414} = 255$ V.

marking_scheme.step: Distance 0.141 m and algebraic sum 4 nC

questions.stem_md: A charge of 5 μC is carried along a closed path that lies entirely on an equipotential surface at 200 V. The work done is
questions.solution_md: Every step is between points at the same potential, so $W = q\Delta V = 0$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The angle between an electric field line and an equipotential surface at the point where they meet is
questions.solution_md: If $\vec E$ had a component along the surface, work would be done moving along it — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In a uniform field, equipotential planes at 10 V intervals are 2.0 cm apart. Find the field strength, in V m⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{\Delta V}{d} = \dfrac{10}{0.020} = 500$ V m$^{-1}$, pointing towards lower potential.

questions.stem_md: Along the x-axis the potential is $V = 4x^2$ volts, with $x$ in metres. The electric field at $x = 1$ m is

options.text_md: 8 V m$^{-1}$ along the negative x-direction
8 V m$^{-1}$ along the positive x-direction
4 V m$^{-1}$ along the negative x-direction

questions.solution_md: $E_x = -\dfrac{dV}{dx} = -8x = -8$ V m$^{-1}$ at $x = 1$ m — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two different equipotential surfaces can never intersect.

**Reason (R):** At a point of intersection the potential would have two different values.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R is exactly the reason for A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? For an isolated point charge, equipotential surfaces drawn for equal steps of potential are equally spaced.
questions.solution_md: False. $V \propto 1/r$, so equal steps of $V$ need bigger and bigger steps of $r$: the surfaces spread out away from the charge.

questions.stem_md: Match each charge arrangement in Column A with the shape of its equipotential surfaces in Column B.

match_right.text_md: Closed surfaces round each charge, with a flat V = 0 plane midway

questions.solution_md: Point charge → spheres (1 → r); uniform field → planes (2 → p); wire → coaxial cylinders (3 → s); dipole → closed surfaces with a zero plane (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: In a region of space the electric potential has the same value everywhere. The electric field in that region is

options.text_md: equal to the potential divided by the size of the region

questions.solution_md: $E = -dV/dl = 0$ when $V$ does not change — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Explain why the electric field at any point is perpendicular to the equipotential surface through that point.

answer.model_answer_md: Moving a charge along an equipotential takes **no work**, since $\Delta V = 0$. If the field had a component **along** the surface, that component would do work on a charge moved along it. So the field can have **no tangential component**: it must be perpendicular to the surface.

questions.solution_md: Argue from W = qΔV = 0 along the surface.

marking_scheme.step: So no tangential field component: E is perpendicular

questions.stem_md: Find the electrostatic potential energy of a system of charges +2.0 μC and −3.0 μC placed 30 cm apart in air, in joules.
questions.solution_md: $U = \dfrac{kq_1q_2}{r} = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times (-3.0 \times 10^{-6})}{0.30} = -0.18$ J (negative: the system is bound).

questions.stem_md: Charges of +5.0 nC and −2.0 nC are 10 cm apart. The minimum work needed to pull them apart to a very large separation is
questions.solution_md: $U = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 5.0 \times 10^{-9} \times (-2.0 \times 10^{-9})}{0.10} = -9.0 \times 10^{-7}$ J. Final $U = 0$, so $W = 0 - U = 9.0 \times 10^{-7}$ J — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Four equal charges $q$ are at the corners of a square of side $a$. The potential energy of the system is
questions.solution_md: Six pairs: four sides (distance $a$) and two diagonals (distance $a\sqrt{2}$). $U = \dfrac{kq^2}{a}\left(4 + \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \dfrac{kq^2}{a}(4 + \sqrt{2})$ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A dipole of moment 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ C m is aligned with a uniform field of 5.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. Find the work needed to turn it through 180°, in millijoules (mJ).
The potential energy of an electric dipole in a uniform field is least when the angle between $\vec p$ and $\vec E$ is
questions.solution_md: $U = -pE\cos\theta$ is most negative at $\theta = 0^\circ$ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 100 V. The kinetic energy it gains is
questions.solution_md: $K = eV = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 100 = 1.6 \times 10^{-17}$ J, i.e. 100 eV — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A charge of −2.0 μC is placed at a point where the potential due to other charges is +300 V. Its potential energy there is
questions.solution_md: $U = qV = -2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 300 = -6.0 \times 10^{-4}$ J — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The electrostatic potential energy of a system of two unlike charges is negative.

**Reason (R):** Unlike charges repel each other.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true ($q_1q_2 < 0$ in $kq_1q_2/r$). R is false: unlike charges attract — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Charges of +1.0 μC, −2.0 μC and +3.0 μC are fixed on the x-axis at $x = 0$, $x = 10$ cm and $x = 30$ cm. Find the potential energy of the system and say what its sign means.

answer.model_answer_md:
Pairs: $(1, 2)$ at 0.10 m, $(1, 3)$ at 0.30 m, $(2, 3)$ at 0.20 m.
$U = 9 \times 10^{9} \times 10^{-12} \times \left(\dfrac{1 \times (-2)}{0.10} + \dfrac{1 \times 3}{0.30} + \dfrac{(-2) \times 3}{0.20}\right) = 9 \times 10^{-3} \times (-20 + 10 - 30) = -0.36$ J.
**Negative:** an external agent must supply 0.36 J to separate the charges to infinity; the arrangement is bound.

questions.solution_md: Sum kq_iq_j/r_ij over the three pairs.

questions.stem_md: Two protons are brought closer together. Does the potential energy of the system increase or decrease? What happens for a proton and an electron brought closer together? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: For two protons $q_1q_2 > 0$, so $U = kq_1q_2/r$ is positive and **increases** as $r$ decreases: work must be done against the repulsion. For a proton and an electron $q_1q_2 < 0$, so $U$ is negative and becomes **more negative (decreases)** as they approach: the attraction does the work.

questions.solution_md: Use the sign of q₁q₂ in U = kq₁q₂/r.

marking_scheme.step: Two protons: U increases, with reason
Proton and electron: U decreases, with reason

questions.stem_md: True or false? The electric field inside a charge-free cavity in a conductor is zero even when the conductor is charged or placed in an external field.
questions.solution_md: True. This is electrostatic shielding: the charges on the conductor arrange themselves so that the field in the charge-free cavity is zero.

questions.stem_md: Excess charge given to an isolated conductor in electrostatic equilibrium
questions.solution_md: Any charge inside would create a field inside, which must be zero in equilibrium — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The surface charge density on a region of a charged conductor is 1.77 μC m⁻². Find the field just outside that region, in kN C⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{1.77 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.0 \times 10^{5}$ N C$^{-1}$, normal to the surface. In kN C$^{-1}$: $2.0 \times 10^{5}/10^{3} = 200$.

questions.stem_md: Two charged metal spheres of radii 1 cm and 3 cm, far apart, are joined by a thin wire. In the final state, the ratio of their surface charge densities $\sigma_1 : \sigma_2$ is
questions.solution_md: Joined, they reach the same potential: $\dfrac{kq_1}{r_1} = \dfrac{kq_2}{r_2}$, so $q \propto r$. Then $\sigma = \dfrac{q}{4\pi r^2} \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$, giving $\sigma_1 : \sigma_2 = 3 : 1$ — option (a). The smaller sphere has the denser charge, as at the pointed end of a conductor.

questions.stem_md: A bird sits with both feet on a single bare high-voltage line at 11 kV. It is not harmed because

options.text_md: the potential of the line is zero where it sits
both its feet are at practically the same potential, so almost no current flows through it
the current in the line is too small to matter

questions.solution_md: Current through the bird needs a potential difference between its feet; on one wire the two points are at nearly the same potential — option (c). Touching the line and a pole (earth) at once would be fatal.

questions.stem_md: A point charge $+q$ is placed at the centre of an uncharged, isolated, hollow metal sphere. The charges that appear on the inner and outer surfaces of the sphere are

options.text_md: $+q$ on the inner surface and $-q$ on the outer surface
$-q$ on the inner surface and $+q$ on the outer surface
$-q$ on the inner surface and zero on the outer surface

questions.solution_md: A Gaussian surface inside the metal has $E = 0$, so it must enclose zero net charge: the inner surface carries $-q$. The sphere is uncharged, so $+q$ appears on the outer surface — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is made of polar molecules?
questions.solution_md: A water molecule has a permanent dipole moment because of its bent shape; O₂, H₂ and the symmetric CO₂ molecule do not — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An isolated parallel-plate capacitor has a field of $3.0 \times 10^{4}$ V m$^{-1}$ between its plates. A dielectric of constant 6 fills the gap. The field in the dielectric is
questions.solution_md: Charge fixed, so $E = E_0/K = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{4}}{6} = 5.0 \times 10^{3}$ V m$^{-1}$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a charged pear-shaped conductor, the surface charge density is greatest

options.text_md: at the centre of the conductor
at the sharply curved, pointed end

questions.solution_md: Charge density is larger where the radius of curvature is smaller; this is why lightning conductors have points — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Inserting a dielectric slab between the plates of an isolated charged capacitor reduces the field between the plates.

**Reason (R):** The polarised slab has bound surface charges whose field opposes the applied field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and the opposing field of the bound charges is why the net field falls to $E_0/K$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The potential at every point inside a charged hollow conducting sphere is zero.

**Reason (R):** The electric field at every point inside a charged hollow conducting sphere is zero.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: zero field means the potential is constant inside, equal to the surface value $kq/R$, not zero — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between polar and non-polar dielectrics, and explain how each becomes polarised in an external field.

answer.model_answer_md: **Polar** molecules (water) have a **permanent** dipole moment; normally the dipoles point randomly, and a field **aligns** them partly. **Non-polar** molecules (oxygen) have **no** permanent dipole; the field pushes electrons and nuclei slightly apart and **induces** a dipole along the field. In both, the material gains a net dipole moment per unit volume.

questions.solution_md: Contrast permanent and induced dipoles.

marking_scheme.step: Polar: permanent dipoles aligned by the field
Non-polar: dipoles induced by the field

questions.stem_md: During a thunderstorm a student argues that sitting inside a closed metal car is safer than standing under a tall tree. Evaluate the argument using the properties of conductors.

answer.model_answer_md: The argument is **sound**. The car body is a closed **conductor**: the charge stays on its outer surface and the field inside is **zero** (shielding), so no current passes through the people. A tall tree attracts strikes, and current can jump from it to a person nearby.

questions.solution_md: Apply shielding by a closed conductor; compare with the tree.

marking_scheme.step: Car: closed conductor, zero field inside (shielding)
Tree: attracts strikes, current can reach the person

questions.stem_md: Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{1}{6} = 1$, so $C = 1\,\mu\text{F}$, smaller than the smallest — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Two 4 μF capacitors in series are connected in parallel with a 2 μF capacitor. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.solution_md: The series pair gives 2 μF; in parallel with 2 μF the total is 4 μF — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A technician has three identical 2 μF capacitors and needs a capacitance of 3 μF. She should connect

options.text_md: two in series, and the third in parallel with that pair
two in parallel, and the third in series with that pair

questions.solution_md: Two in series give 1 μF; adding 2 μF in parallel gives 3 μF — option (c). (All series: 0.67 μF; all parallel: 6 μF; parallel pair in series with one: 1.33 μF.)

questions.stem_md: A parallel-plate capacitor has plates of area 50 cm² separated by 2.0 mm of air. Find its capacitance, in picofarads.
The plate separation of a parallel-plate capacitor of capacitance $C$ is halved and the gap is filled with a dielectric of constant 3. The new capacitance is

answer.model_answer_md:
Let the charges $-q$ and $+q$ be at distances $r_2$ and $r_1$ from P. $V = \dfrac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$. questions.stem_md: (a) Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor with air between the plates. (b) How does it change when the gap is completely filled with a dielectric of constant $K$? (c) Plates of area 400 cm² are 2.0 mm apart. Find the capacitance in air and with a dielectric of $K = 4$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Let the plates have area $A$, separation $d$ and charges $\pm Q$, so $\sigma = Q/A$. Each plate acts as a large sheet with field $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$. **Between** the plates the two fields point the same way and add: $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0 A}$; outside they cancel. The field is uniform, so $V = Ed = \dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0 A}$. Hence $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.

(b) The polarised dielectric reduces the field (for the same $Q$) to $E/K$, so $V$ falls $K$ times and $C = \dfrac{K\varepsilon_0 A}{d}$.

(c) $A = 400 \times 10^{-4} = 0.040$ m². $C_0 = \dfrac{8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.040}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.77 \times 10^{-10}$ F (177 pF). With $K = 4$: $C = 4 \times 177 = 708$ pF.

questions.solution_md: Field between plates σ/ε₀, V = Ed, C = Q/V; then multiply by K.

marking_scheme.step: Field between plates σ/ε₀, zero outside
With dielectric C = Kε₀A/d, with reason

Explain the difference in the energy changes.

answer.model_answer_md:
Initially $Q_0 = C_0V_0 = 10 \times 100 = 1000\,\mu\text{C}$ and $U_0 = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10^{-6} \times 100^2 = 0.050$ J.

(a) **Connected (V fixed):** $C = 50\,\mu\text{F}$, $V = 100$ V, $Q = 50 \times 100 = 5000\,\mu\text{C}$, $U = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 50 \times 10^{-6} \times 100^2 = 0.25$ J (5 times larger).

(b) **Disconnected (Q fixed):** $C = 50\,\mu\text{F}$, $Q = 1000\,\mu\text{C}$, $V = 1000/50 = 20$ V, $U = \dfrac{(10^{-3})^2}{2 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = 0.010$ J (5 times smaller).

**Why:** in (a) the battery moves an extra 4000 μC through 100 V, doing 0.40 J of work; 0.20 J of it raises the stored energy and the rest is the work done on the slab as it is pulled in. In (b) no energy is supplied, and the field does work pulling the slab in, so the stored energy falls.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Q fixed, V = 20 V, U = 0.010 J

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that the potential energy of an electric dipole of moment $\vec p$ at angle $\theta$ to a uniform field $\vec E$ is $U = -pE\cos\theta$ (taking $U = 0$ at $\theta = 90^\circ$). (b) State the positions of stable and unstable equilibrium. (c) A dipole of moment $2.0 \times 10^{-8}$ C m is turned from $0^\circ$ to $60^\circ$ in a field of $3.0 \times 10^{4}$ N C$^{-1}$. Find the work done.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The torque on the dipole is $\tau = pE\sin\theta$, tending to reduce $\theta$. To turn it slowly through $d\theta$, an external agent does work $dW = pE\sin\theta\,d\theta$. From $90^\circ$ to $\theta$: $W = \int_{90^\circ}^{\theta} pE\sin\theta\,d\theta = pE(\cos 90^\circ - \cos\theta) = -pE\cos\theta$. This work is stored as potential energy: $U(\theta) = -pE\cos\theta = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$.

(b) **Stable** at $\theta = 0^\circ$ ($U = -pE$, minimum); **unstable** at $\theta = 180^\circ$ ($U = +pE$, maximum).

(c) $W = pE(\cos 0^\circ - \cos 60^\circ) = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \times 3.0 \times 10^{4} \times 0.5 = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ J.

questions.solution_md: Integrate the torque over the angle; then use W = pE(cos θ₁ − cos θ₂).

marking_scheme.step: Work dW = pE sin θ dθ against the torque

questions.stem_md: (a) State four properties of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, giving a reason for each. (b) Explain electrostatic shielding and give one practical use. (c) Find the field just outside a conductor where the surface charge density is 2.655 μC m⁻².

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) **$E = 0$ inside:** free electrons would otherwise move. (ii) **Excess charge on the surface:** a Gaussian surface just inside the surface has zero field, so encloses zero charge. (iii) **$E$ normal to the surface outside:** a tangential component would move surface charges. (iv) **The conductor is an equipotential:** no field inside or along the surface means no work in moving a charge from point to point.

(b) Inside a **charge-free cavity** of a conductor the field is zero, whatever charges or fields are outside. Uses: sensitive instruments are kept in metal cases; a closed car protects passengers from lightning.

(c) $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{2.655 \times 10^{-6}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}} = 3.0 \times 10^{5}$ N C$^{-1}$, normal to the surface.

questions.solution_md: List the equilibrium properties with reasons; shielding from zero field in a cavity; E = σ/ε₀.

questions.stem_md: (a) Derive the expression for the equivalent capacitance of capacitors connected (i) in series, (ii) in parallel. (b) Capacitors of 6 μF and 12 μF in series are connected in parallel with a 4 μF capacitor across a 24 V supply. Find the total charge drawn from the supply and the energy stored in the network.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a)(i) **Series:** each capacitor carries the same $Q$, and the voltages add: $V = V_1 + V_2 + \dots = Q\left(\dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dots\right)$. With $V = Q/C$: $\dfrac{1}{C} = \dfrac{1}{C_1} + \dfrac{1}{C_2} + \dots$
(ii) **Parallel:** each has the same $V$, and the charges add: $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 + \dots = (C_1 + C_2 + \dots)V$, so $C = C_1 + C_2 + \dots$

(b) Series pair: $\dfrac{6 \times 12}{6 + 12} = 4\,\mu\text{F}$; total $C = 4 + 4 = 8\,\mu\text{F}$. Total charge $Q = 8 \times 24 = 192\,\mu\text{C}$. Energy $U = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 10^{-6} \times 24^2 = 2.30 \times 10^{-3}$ J.

questions.solution_md: Same Q in series, same V in parallel; then reduce the network.

The air would break down and **spark** long before then, so it is **not possible** with this sphere; a larger sphere would be needed.

alternatives.solution_md: Compare V/R with the breakdown field.

marking_scheme.step: Exceeds breakdown, so not possible (larger sphere needed)
